While I like the idea in principle I can already think of a whole bucket list of pitfalls that would make this a little bit hard to justify implementing:

- Sync would be essentially impossible because without insight into the video stream there is no way to account for adverts and buffering speed

- To be able to handle any of YouTube's official player implementations something akin to an entire browser would need to be run alongside VRChat, which would be slow on PC and potentially outright impossible on Quest

- The intrinsically non-human behaviour of simply loading videos and not interacting with them is likely to trip bot detection anyway, requesting either a captcha or sign-in

- If you give people a means to interact with the container to pass captchas or sign in then you open the door for inevitably being able to escape the sandbox

Discord has their "watch together" functionality, but that is the product of what I believe to be a private and quite expensive contract made directly with YouTube. Even so if you've used it you might have found, much as I have, that it's a relatively unpolished and unpleasant experience, almost always inferior to just screen sharing a browser with YouTube open.

Having yt-dlp break every so often feels like a QoL issue but I think this solution is too likely to spawn into several more potentially worse QoL issues. I think it's better for it to either work great or not work entirely than for it to *always* work with several caveats (and this is unlikely to always work).

Thanks, this is genuinely useful pushback and I think you're right on most of it. To be clear, I wasn't picturing a full browser-parity official player — more something narrower, like a restricted/sandboxed embed just for playback (no interaction beyond play/pause/seek), similar in spirit to how a game console's YouTube app works rather than a full browser tab. But I take your point that even that minimal surface still runs into the same core issues:

Ad/buffer sync without stream visibility is a real blocker regardless of how thin the embed is

Any container capable enough to pass a captcha or sign-in is capable enough to be a sandbox escape risk

Quest feasibility alone probably kills it even if PC could handle it

The Discord Watch Together point is a good real-world data point too — if a company with an actual paid deal and dedicated engineering resources still ships something that feels worse than screen-sharing a browser, that's a strong signal this isn't just an implementation-effort problem, it's closer to a fundamental one.

I think your closing point is the one that sticks with me most: "work great or not work at all" vs. "always works but with caveats." Right now yt-dlp-based playback sits in an uncomfortable middle — it mostly works, but every YouTube-side change threatens to (temporarily) break it, and there's no way to fully control for that as a third party. I don't have a fix for that, I mostly just wanted the pitfalls to be visible in one place in case anyone with actual access ever revisits this. Appreciate you laying them out this clearly.

> For example, YouTube provides an official embedded player through the IFrame Player API.

This requires solving a JavaScript challenge for playback, or in other words executing a snippet of code provided by YouTube (with plausible security implications). VRChat's yt-dlp fork uses a custom `vrcrustyscript` JavaScript runtime. The upstream yt-dlp project generally uses Deno. This also relies on yt-dlp-ejs (which requires updates from time to time).

I don't think it's too different than running yt-dlp with a different playback path using this embedded client with `--extractor-args youtube:player_client=web_embedded`.

The benefit of using yt-dlp is also that it supports over 900 different services, as of yt-dlp 2026.07.04. https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp/tree/2026.07.04/yt_dlp/extractor

yt-dlp is also auto-updated when the user switches worlds.

A hypothetical unique playback path/executable for YouTube would need to be engineered, maintained, and updated by VRChat - ideally with over-the-air (OTA) updates like yt-dlp, without a full client update. It sounds like a hard ask over the current situation of using yt-dlp, which also supports the `web_embedded` player.

Imo a better idea may be to give the VRChat community access to VRChat's yt-dlp changes and develop it like any free software project out in the open. https://feedback.vrchat.com/feature-requests/p/publish-yt-dlp-modifications

details:
I would like to propose exploring an official YouTube playback method for VRChat that does not depend on extracting direct media URLs with yt-dlp.

I am an independent developer who maintains a community tool related to YouTube video playback in VRChat. The tool has received more than 9,000 downloads across its releases, which has given me a firsthand view of the demand for reliable YouTube playback in VRChat.

Recent updates addressing YouTube playback issues have also seen significant download activity shortly after release.

While maintaining this tool, I have repeatedly encountered the same fundamental issue: YouTube changes its playback and anti-automation systems, which can cause yt-dlp-based playback to stop working or become limited. The solution is then usually to wait for yt-dlp to adapt and for VRChat to update its bundled version.

I understand that VRChat itself currently uses yt-dlp to resolve URLs for video players, and I am not suggesting that yt-dlp is a bad solution. It works well when compatible with YouTube's current behavior.

However, I wonder whether VRChat could eventually provide an alternative, official playback path that relies on YouTube's own player rather than extracting a direct media stream URL.

For example, YouTube provides an official embedded player through the IFrame Player API. In a normal Unity application, this could potentially be displayed through a WebView or similar browser-based component. I understand that VRChat's current Udon sandbox and platform architecture may make this difficult or impossible, especially considering security, performance, and Quest compatibility.

I am therefore not specifically asking for a general-purpose WebView.

Rather, I would like to suggest investigating whether VRChat could provide a restricted and secure mechanism for official video embeds, or another architecture that allows YouTube itself to handle playback without VRChat having to continuously adapt to YouTube's internal streaming implementation.

The goal would not necessarily be to replace yt-dlp immediately, but to provide a long-term alternative for YouTube playback that is less dependent on YouTube's internal APIs and extraction behavior.

I would also be very interested to know whether VRChat has previously considered such an approach, and if not, whether there are technical or security limitations that would make it impractical.

Thank you for considering this proposal.
title: Explore an official YouTube playback method independent of yt-dlp
